paragraphs: The paper studies how to predict positive or negative labels on network links while asking for relatively few labels. Its active learning algorithms choose which edges to query, then use the information to classify other edges. The analysis assumes a stochastic model: an initial assignment of signs agrees with a division of the nodes into two groups, and perturbations introduce deviations from that assignment.

Within this model, the authors establish a strong guarantee for graphs with at least order |V|^(3/2) edges. Querying at most order |V|^(3/2) labels is enough to achieve a mistake count within a constant factor of optimal. This connects the amount of supervision to the number of nodes, even when the graph contains many more edges.

A more general algorithm exposes a tradeoff controlled by k: it queries at most order |V| + (|V|/k)^(3/2) labels and achieves optimality within a factor of order k. Its running time is at most order |E| + |V| log |V|, making computational efficiency part of the contribution alongside label efficiency.
neurips-2012-a-linear-time-active-learni.tldr: Active learning algorithms classify signed network links efficiently, with model-dependent guarantees that trade label queries against prediction mistakes.

paragraphs: P300 spelling interfaces face two practical obstacles: users may need lengthy training sessions, and the system may require many repetitions of the same stimulus. This paper introduces unsupervised hierarchical probabilistic models designed to address both obstacles together. The aim is to make spelling usable without first collecting a dedicated supervised training session from the current user.

The models incorporate two sources of prior information. Transfer learning supplies information from other training subjects, while language models supply information about the words being spelled. These sources bring both experience from other people and expectations about language into the interpretation of the spelling signals.

The authors report that the resulting unsupervised models perform comparably to supervised models and sometimes exceed them, while eliminating the training session. The finding supports the value of combining prior knowledge across users and words: supervision gathered elsewhere can help make an interface usable immediately. The reported advantage is qualified, with performance matching supervised methods generally and surpassing them only in some cases.
neurips-2012-a-p300-bci-for-the-masses-p.tldr: Combining information from other users with language models enables unsupervised P300 spelling that can match or sometimes surpass supervised performance.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a method for classifying functional MRI data when the prediction task contains tens of classes. Its central design choice is to draw on information from as many brain locations as possible. That matters for semantic analysis because the method is intended to use the wider activation pattern, rather than first narrowing the input through feature selection.

The approach decomposes brain activation into subregions that differ in how informative they are. This gives the classifier a way to organize a broad collection of brain measurements while acknowledging that different regions contribute different amounts of predictive information. Keeping a wide spatial scope therefore does not require treating every location as equally useful.

Results on a complex semantic processing dataset show performance competitive with state-of-the-art feature selection. The findings suggest that this decomposition can preserve useful predictive information without relying on the usual selection step. They also suggest possible applications to group analysis and exploration of relationships among many classes; these are proposed uses rather than established general conclusions about brain organization.
neurips-2012-a-systematic-approach-to-ex.tldr: A classifier organizes fMRI activation into differently informative subregions, using broad brain coverage while achieving competitive semantic classification.

paragraphs: The paper explores how to use continuous mathematical representations for probabilistic inference in models whose variables are discrete. Continuous relaxations already have a role in discrete optimization, but the authors identify approximate inference as a less explored application. Their contribution is a transformation that makes a wide class of discrete undirected models accessible to continuous inference techniques.

The transformation uses a general form of the Gaussian Integral Trick to construct fully continuous systems. This representation allows gradient-based Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to be used for inference. The key benefit is methodological: changing the representation makes a different collection of computational tools available for studying the original discrete system.

The continuous formulation also provides new approaches to estimating partition functions, the normalization constants needed to turn model weights into probabilities. The authors demonstrate some of the resulting inference algorithms on illustrative problems. These demonstrations support the usefulness of the connection, while the broader contribution is the set of inference possibilities created by moving between discrete models and continuous representations.
neurips-2012-continuous-relaxations-for-.tldr: A Gaussian integral transformation enables continuous inference methods, including Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, for a wide class of discrete undirected models.

paragraphs: Maximum marginal prediction chooses the most probable state of each variable in a probabilistic graphical model. It is relevant, for example, when errors are counted separately for each predicted variable through Hamming loss. The usual workflow estimates marginal probabilities first and makes decisions afterward, potentially continuing inference even where the eventual prediction is already sufficiently clear.

The authors propose tracking uncertainty about each decision directly during sampling. Once confidence in an individual decision is sufficient, its variable is dynamically pruned from the factor graph. Subsequent sampling then focuses on variables whose decisions remain uncertain, so the amount of work adapts as more predictions become settled.

Experiments on multi-label classification and image inpainting show that this adaptive allocation of samples can substantially accelerate prediction without reducing accuracy. The result highlights a useful distinction between estimating probabilities and obtaining confident decisions: the latter can sometimes be accomplished earlier. The reported speed and accuracy findings come from these experimental settings, where pruning allowed computation to concentrate on unresolved predictions.
neurips-2012-dynamic-pruning-of-factor-g.tldr: Dynamically removing sufficiently confident decisions from a factor graph can accelerate sampling-based prediction without sacrificing accuracy in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Bayesian nonparametric sequence models can represent an unknown number of activity patterns, but inference must explore that flexible model space efficiently. This paper develops Markov chain Monte Carlo methods for the beta process hidden Markov model. The application is discovering patterns shared across video and motion capture sequences, including behaviors that appear only rarely.

The methods introduce split and merge proposals based on sequential allocation, allowing large changes to the shared feature structure. They also use data-driven reversible jump proposals to discover rare or unique behaviors more reliably. Together, these proposals address both reorganizing common patterns and finding patterns with little representation in the observations.

The proposals apply to conjugate observation likelihoods, with demonstrations using multinomial, Gaussian, and autoregressive emissions. The authors report tractable analysis of hundreds of time series. For comparison, previous inference required careful initialization and at least ten thousand burn-in iterations for only six sequences. The stated improvement is therefore about making the flexible model practical at a much larger collection size.
neurips-2012-effective-split-merge-monte.tldr: New split-merge and reversible jump proposals make inference in beta process hidden Markov models practical for hundreds of time series.

paragraphs: The paper studies the reliability of estimating Shannon mutual information, a quantity that measures statistical dependence between variables. It proves an exponential concentration inequality for a plug-in estimator. This type of result controls the probability that an estimate departs substantially from its target, going beyond a guarantee about average estimation error.

That distinction becomes important when many pairs of variables must be considered together. Earlier results described in the abstract bounded expected error, whereas the new inequality can be combined with a union bound to guarantee accuracy across many pairwise estimates simultaneously. The contribution therefore connects the reliability of individual estimates to the reliability of a larger collection of dependence measurements.

As an application, the authors use the result to optimally estimate both a density and its graph when the underlying distribution is Markov with respect to a forest. The forest assumption defines the setting of this application. The main significance is that stronger control of estimation error supports learning an entire graphical structure, alongside the probability distribution associated with it.
neurips-2012-exponential-concentration-f.tldr: An exponential error bound for mutual information estimates enables simultaneous guarantees across variable pairs and optimal estimation for forest-structured distributions.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation studies learning when the data used for training and the domain of interest differ. This paper develops a framework for analyzing generalization in two representative settings: learning from multiple source domains, and learning with a combination of source and target data. The goal is to characterize how the learning process behaves as more data become available.

The framework introduces two quantities that describe inherent characteristics of the domains. Using these quantities, the authors derive deviation and symmetrization inequalities tailored to each setting. These lead to generalization bounds based on the uniform entropy number, which serves as a way to account for the complexity of the functions being learned.

The resulting bounds are then used to analyze asymptotic convergence and convergence rates, as well as factors that influence long-run behavior. Numerical experiments support the theoretical results. The contribution is an analytical framework connecting domain characteristics and learning complexity to generalization, giving a way to study both multiple-source adaptation and the use of target data within a common approach.
neurips-2012-generalization-bounds-for-d.tldr: A theoretical framework derives generalization and convergence bounds for adaptation from multiple sources or combined source and target data.

paragraphs: This paper studies how accurately data can be used to estimate a probability measure when error is assessed using optimal transport metrics. The measure is assumed to be supported on a manifold embedded in a Hilbert space. This places the estimation problem in a geometric setting, where the structure of the space supporting the data is part of the analysis.

The authors establish a connection between optimal transport, optimal quantization, and learning theory. They use this connection to obtain probabilistic performance bounds for k-means when its output is used to construct a probability measure from observations. This gives the familiar clustering algorithm an additional interpretation as a tool for approximating an underlying distribution.

The analysis also produces new lower bounds and probabilistic convergence-rate bounds for the empirical law of large numbers. The authors state that the latter apply to a broad class of measures beyond the reach of existing bounds. The findings connect practical distribution approximation with theoretical limits and guarantees on how empirical distributions approach their underlying measures.
neurips-2012-learning-probability-measur.tldr: Connections between optimal transport, quantization, and learning theory yield new guarantees for k-means as a probability-measure estimator.

paragraphs: Conventional supervised regression learns from inputs paired with their target outputs. This paper investigates a different source of training information: a probability model describing the target variables, together with inputs that lack corresponding targets. The proposed scheme, learning with target priors, uses this distributional knowledge to estimate the relationship between inputs and outputs.

The method chooses the parameters of a regressor so that its predictions on the unpaired training inputs have high likelihood under the target prior. This makes prior knowledge about plausible outputs directly influence learning. Its usefulness depends on having a model of the targets that can supply information otherwise obtained from paired examples.

The authors argue that this approach can reduce or remove reliance on conventional training data and can produce a regressor suited to efficient deployment. They demonstrate effectiveness on brain-computer interface signal decoding and pose estimation from video. The efficiency claim is especially relevant to online decoding, where the learned mapping must be applied quickly, while the central learning contribution is the use of target distributions as supervision.
neurips-2012-learning-with-target-prior-.tldr: Learning with target priors trains a parametric regressor from unpaired inputs by making its outputs likely under a known target distribution.

paragraphs: Matching keypoints across images requires a compact description of each surrounding image patch. Such descriptors support recognition, image mosaicing, and structure from motion, but their computation can be costly for real-time mobile use. This paper introduces LUCID, a simple descriptor intended to combine inexpensive computation with strong matching accuracy.

LUCID compares the ordering of RGB intensity values in two patches using permutation distances. Its computation grows linearly with patch size and does not require floating point arithmetic. This differs from BRIEF and related methods, which describe patches through randomly sampled pairwise intensity comparisons. The authors also provide an analysis identifying an issue that limits those methods relative to LUCID.

In the reported experiments, LUCID is faster than BRIEF. Its accuracy is directly comparable to SURF while its speed exceeds SURF by more than an order of magnitude. These results make the intensity-ordering representation practically significant: the descriptor achieves a favorable combination of speed and accuracy in the evaluations, rather than requiring accuracy to be sacrificed simply to obtain cheap computation.
neurips-2012-locally-uniform-comparison-.tldr: LUCID compares patch intensity orderings, achieving SURF-comparable accuracy at more than ten times its speed in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Conditional Markov chains, also called linear-chain conditional random fields, model a sequence of hidden states given a sequence of observed variables. This paper develops their statistical theory, extending earlier work on large-sample properties. Its focus is on understanding the behavior of the model and its parameter estimates as a mathematical object.

The first contribution establishes mixing properties for models with unbounded feature functions. Mixing describes how dependence weakens across a sequence, while unbounded features need not stay within a fixed finite range. Addressing these features extends the theoretical analysis to a setting in which that boundedness restriction is unavailable.

The second contribution gives necessary conditions for model identifiability and uniqueness of maximum likelihood estimates. Identifiability concerns whether the observable distribution can distinguish different parameter choices; uniqueness concerns whether likelihood maximization selects a single estimate. Necessary conditions identify requirements that must hold for these properties, without asserting that those requirements alone guarantee them. Together, the results strengthen the foundations for reasoning about dependence and parameter estimation in conditional sequence models.
neurips-2012-mixing-properties-of-condit.tldr: The paper establishes mixing properties with unbounded features and necessary conditions for identifiability and unique maximum likelihood estimates in conditional Markov chains.

paragraphs: Some prediction systems can return several candidate answers because a user or later component can rank them and select the best. This paper studies how to learn for that setting when each answer is a structured output. The value of the returned collection depends on the useful choices it offers to the downstream selector.

A conventional approach trains one model and extracts its M most probable predictions. The authors instead formulate learning itself as a multiple-output structured prediction problem. They define a loss that reflects the multiple-choice setting and develop a max-margin formulation that minimizes an upper bound on that loss. The training objective therefore accounts for the intended use of several hypotheses.

Experiments on image co-segmentation and protein side-chain prediction show substantial accuracy improvements over conventional approaches for this scenario. These results support training explicitly for collections of outputs when a later stage can identify the best candidate. The ability to rank the returned hypotheses is part of the problem setup and explains why multiple-choice learning can be useful.
neurips-2012-multiple-choice-learning-le.tldr: Training directly to produce multiple structured predictions improves accuracy in settings where a user or downstream component can select the best candidate.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning how variables influence one another over continuous time. Continuous-time Bayesian networks can represent these dependencies, but their conditional intensity matrices become costly as a variable gains more parents. The number of matrices grows exponentially with the parent count, creating a barrier to modeling richer dependency structures.

The authors introduce a partition-based representation built from regression trees and forests. Its parameter space grows linearly with the number of node splits, giving model complexity a different basis from enumerating parent configurations. Under a multiplicative assumption, the forest likelihood can be updated in closed form, enabling efficient changes to the model during learning.

The reported results show that multiplicative forests can be learned from only a few temporal trajectories, with large gains in performance and scalability. The contribution combines a compact way to represent conditional behavior with a convenient likelihood update. The multiplicative assumption is central to the computational result: it supplies the structure that makes those closed-form updates possible.
neurips-2012-multiplicative-forests-for-.tldr: Multiplicative regression forests provide a scalable representation of continuous-time dependencies with closed-form likelihood updates under a multiplicative assumption.

paragraphs: Matrix factorization represents collaborative prediction data using latent factors, but the appropriate number of factors may be unknown. This paper presents a probabilistic formulation of max-margin matrix factorization and uses it to build a Bayesian nonparametric model. The resulting model automatically resolves how many latent factors are needed within its modeling framework.

The contribution brings together two approaches usually treated separately: max-margin learning and Bayesian nonparametrics. The former supplies the margin-based learning formulation, while the latter provides flexibility over the unknown latent dimension. Their integration lets the model address prediction and representation size as connected parts of the same learning problem.

The authors develop an efficient variational algorithm for posterior inference, making the combined formulation computationally usable. Extensive experiments use the large-scale MovieLens and EachMovie datasets. The authors describe those findings as appearing to support the complementary advantages of the two approaches. The evidence therefore supports the proposed integration while retaining a qualified claim about the benefits demonstrated by the empirical studies.
neurips-2012-nonparametric-max-margin-ma.tldr: A Bayesian nonparametric formulation combines max-margin matrix factorization with automatic selection of the latent factor count.

paragraphs: Latent variable models explain data through unobserved structure, such as mixture components or topics. Their priors often treat internal parameters as independent and identically distributed, allowing redundant components without expressing a preference against overlap. This paper asks whether diversity should be built into the prior itself so that the learned representation contains more distinct elements.

The authors replace the independent prior with a determinantal point process. A positive definite kernel expresses the desired notion of diversity, and a kernel between probability distributions allows the process to operate on probability measures. Diversity thus becomes part of the probabilistic specification rather than a separate criterion applied after learning.

The paper develops maximum a posteriori inference with these priors for latent Dirichlet allocation and mixture models. The reported results provide more intuitive latent representations and quantitatively improve unsupervised feature extraction while preserving the models' generative character. The significance is that a preference for distinct components can be incorporated into familiar probabilistic models and influence the usefulness of their learned features.
neurips-2012-priors-for-diversity-in-gen.tldr: Determinantal point process priors encourage diverse latent components and improve unsupervised feature extraction in topic and mixture models.

paragraphs: Finding a most-probable explanation means choosing the joint assignment favored most strongly by a probabilistic model. In continuous domains, that search can also have to satisfy constraints, making inference computationally expensive. This paper targets the scalability of this task in a particular class of constrained continuous graphical models.

The supported models contain piecewise-linear and piecewise-quadratic dependencies together with linear constraints. The authors derive inference algorithms using a consensus-optimization framework. These structural requirements define the scope of the contribution: the approach takes advantage of a specified mathematical form for both dependencies and restrictions on valid assignments.

The experiments demonstrate better performance than state-of-the-art methods. On a large-scale voter-preference modeling problem, the algorithms empirically scale linearly with the number of dependencies and constraints. That finding suggests that adding more modeled relationships and restrictions can remain manageable in this application. The linear scaling is an experimental observation from the reported problem, while the broader contribution is the consensus-based approach to MPE inference for the stated model class.
neurips-2012-scaling-mpe-inference-for-c.tldr: Consensus optimization accelerates MPE inference for a specified class of constrained continuous graphical models, with empirical linear scaling in voter-preference modeling.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often needs compact representations of very large feature vectors. Hashing maps those vectors into fixed-size tables, but different features can collide in the same location. In value function approximation, these collisions can bias estimates, creating a cost for the memory savings that make hashing attractive.

The paper investigates the tug-of-war sketch, a data structure developed for estimating inner products without bias, as a replacement for standard hashing in linear value approximation. A crucial distinction is that unbiased inner-product estimation does not make the resulting reinforcement learning value estimates unbiased. The authors explicitly find that bias remains in this setting.

Even so, the bias can be orders of magnitude smaller than with standard hashing. Experiments on two reinforcement learning benchmark domains and fifty-five Atari 2600 games demonstrate superior learning performance. The contribution is therefore a more effective way to compress features while reducing the damage associated with collisions, with both the remaining bias and the reported improvements central to interpreting the result.
neurips-2012-sketch-based-linear-value-f.tldr: Tug-of-war sketches reduce the bias of hashed value estimates and improve reinforcement learning performance, although the value estimates remain biased.

paragraphs: Dynamic Markov logic networks describe temporal relationships using weighted logical statements, but changing the time domain can affect their behavior. The paper identifies problems beyond the known dependence of marginal probabilities on domain size: standard construction can also make the underlying Markov chain vary with time. These issues matter when training and testing involve different sets of time points.

The authors additionally examine the cost of sequential inference. Generating samples for the next time slice from previous samples can require estimating a separate normalization factor for each sample, which is expensive in general. They introduce slice normalized dynamic Markov logic networks as a discriminative model that avoids these identified representational and computational issues.

The model supports efficient online inference and can represent relationships within a time slice without assigning them a causal direction. This retains a capability that fully directed models do not directly provide. Experiments show improved accuracy over earlier approaches to online inference in dynamic Markov logic networks, connecting the revised formulation to a demonstrated predictive benefit.
neurips-2012-slice-normalized-dynamic-ma.tldr: Slice normalization addresses identified consistency and sampling problems in dynamic Markov logic while enabling efficient, more accurate online inference in experiments.

paragraphs: Constrained stochastic gradient descent commonly projects each updated solution back into the feasible domain. For complicated domains, such as the positive semidefinite cone, this projection can be expensive enough to undermine the method's appeal for large problems. The paper targets that repeated computational cost while still requiring a feasible final answer.

The authors develop stochastic gradient algorithms that avoid intermediate projections and perform just one projection at the last iteration. This changes when feasibility is enforced: the final projection supplies a solution in the permitted domain without paying for that operation at every step. The computational motivation is strongest when projection itself is costly.

The theoretical analysis gives high-probability convergence rates under mild conditions on the domain and objective. For general convex optimization, the rate is O(1/sqrt(T)); for strongly convex optimization, it is O(ln(T)/T). These guarantees show that eliminating repeated projections can coexist with controlled convergence under the stated conditions. The result is a principled way to reduce projection work while retaining both final feasibility and quantitative optimization guarantees.
neurips-2012-stochastic-gradient-descent.tldr: Stochastic gradient algorithms use only a final projection while retaining high-probability convergence guarantees under conditions on the objective and domain.

paragraphs: Bayesian hierarchical clustering uses a probability model over possible clustering trees. This paper introduces a prior called the Time-Marginalized Coalescent, constructed from Kingman's coalescent by integrating out its time information. The resulting prior describes tree structures without carrying the original timing variables along with them.

This construction allows models to factorize tree structure and times. The separation provides two stated benefits: greater flexibility in constructing priors and access to more efficient Gibbs-type inference. It changes how the hierarchy can be modeled and explored computationally, because the tree's branching structure and its timing information need no longer be tied together in the original way.

The authors demonstrate the approach in an example density-estimation model and report competitive experimental results. This shows that the new prior can support a practical statistical task alongside its structural and computational motivations. The contribution is a reusable choice of prior for nonparametric Bayesian hierarchical clustering, with the density-estimation experiment illustrating its usefulness rather than establishing universal superiority.
neurips-2012-the-time-marginalized-coale.tldr: Integrating time out of Kingman's coalescent yields a flexible tree prior that supports more efficient Gibbs-type hierarchical-clustering inference.

paragraphs: A policy with high expected utility can still perform unacceptably badly under some possible system parameters. This paper studies objectives that express a willingness to give up some average utility to reduce that risk. It uses a Bayesian treatment of parameter uncertainty without requiring a particular distributional form for that uncertainty.

The authors introduce percentile measures, a broad family of robust policy objectives encompassing most existing approaches, including some known to be intractable. They then identify a broad subclass whose robust policies can be approximated efficiently. This distinction matters: the general framework describes many risk preferences, but the efficient approximation result applies to the identified subclass.

For those objectives, the optimization problem is framed as a two-player zero-sum extensive-form game. A no-regret algorithm is used to approximate an optimal policy, with computation polynomial in the number of states and actions of the Markov decision process. The contribution links expressive risk-aware objectives to a computational route for obtaining policies under uncertain action effects.
neurips-2012-tractable-objectives-for-ro.tldr: The paper identifies a broad class of risk-aware policy objectives that admit efficient approximation through a zero-sum game formulation.

paragraphs: Audio classification and retrieval often use discriminative detectors to connect acoustic observations directly to semantic categories. The authors argue that this connection may involve more structure than a direct mapping captures. They introduce a generative model intended to represent a hierarchy between raw acoustic information and higher-level meaning.

The model has two layers. The first represents generic sound units without clear semantic associations, and the second seeks patterns over those units. This makes intermediate structure central to the approach: the basic units need not each correspond to a recognizable concept for their combinations to provide useful information about meaning.

The authors evaluate the model on a large-scale retrieval task from TRECVID 2011 and report significant improvements over standard baselines. Those findings support the usefulness of discovering structure between acoustics and semantics for the evaluated retrieval problem. The conceptual contribution is the hierarchical representation, which allows meaningful patterns to emerge above generic sound units instead of requiring the lowest-level representation to carry semantic labels directly.
neurips-2012-unsupervised-structure-disc.tldr: A two-layer generative audio model discovers patterns over generic sound units and improves retrieval over standard baselines in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Crowdsourced datasets often contain conflicting labels from annotators whose reliability is uncertain. This paper treats aggregation of those labels as an inference problem in a graphical model. It applies approximate methods, including belief propagation and mean field, to turn a collection of unreliable judgments into inferred labels.

The formulation also connects several existing approaches. The proposed belief propagation algorithm generalizes both majority voting and an earlier aggregation algorithm, while the mean-field method is closely related to a commonly used expectation-maximization algorithm. These relationships place familiar methods within a shared inference perspective and help expose choices that affect their behavior.

The authors find that performance depends critically on the prior distribution over worker reliability. With a suitable prior, belief propagation, mean field, and expectation maximization perform strongly on simulated and real-world datasets, remaining competitive with state-of-the-art algorithms using more complicated assumptions. The finding emphasizes that the reliability prior is a consequential modeling choice: good results arise from the combination of inference method and appropriately chosen prior.
neurips-2012-variational-inference-for-c.tldr: Graphical-model inference aggregates crowdsourced labels competitively, with performance critically dependent on the prior over worker reliability.

paragraphs: This paper modifies sparse coding to represent both the absence and intensity of image components more flexibly. It combines a spike-and-slab prior with the nonlinear combination rule of maximal causes analysis. These changes address how individual components are represented and how multiple components jointly generate an image.

Combining the changes creates difficult, strongly multimodal posterior distributions. The authors develop an exact piecewise Gibbs sampler and combine it with a variational method that preselects latent dimensions. This training scheme addresses analytical and computational difficulties while retaining rich posterior structure, enabling models with many observed and hidden dimensions.

Applied to image patches, the model predicts asymmetric, bimodal activity for simple cells in V1 and a high proportion of globular receptive fields alongside Gabor-like fields. Similar proportions of globular fields appear in the neural recordings considered. A consistency check also finds approximate agreement between the average posterior and prior. These results support the proposed flexible priors and nonlinear combinations as improvements to sparse-coding accounts of simple cells, without establishing that the model fully describes biological encoding.
neurips-2012-why-mca-nonlinear-sparse-co.tldr: Efficient inference enables a nonlinear spike-and-slab image model whose predicted activity and receptive fields support a richer sparse-coding account of V1.
